hints: Start by identifying the gas, a gas that turns damp red litmus blue is always alkaline, so think about what it is and how it was formed.
Look at the first reaction in the test tube, $\text{NH}_4^+$ reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ to make $\text{NH}_3$, so ask yourself who donated the proton there.
Now look at the second reaction on the damp paper, $\text{NH}_3$ reacts with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to make $\text{OH}^-$, so ask yourself who donated the proton this time.
walkthrough:
**Identify the gas produced**

Think like a detective. A gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue must be alkaline.

That classic test tells you the gas is ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**Decide the role of the ammonium ion**

Remember, a Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton ($\text{H}^+$) donor and a base is a proton acceptor.

In that test tube reaction, $\text{NH}_4^+$ gives an $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{OH}^-$ to form $\text{NH}_3$. So $\text{NH}_4^+$ is the donor, a Bronsted-Lowry acid.

**Decide the role of water on the litmus paper**

The paper is damp, so the $\text{NH}_3$ gas dissolves in the water on it. This is what actually makes the alkali that changes the colour:
$$\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$
Here $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives an $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{NH}_3$. So water is the donor, a Bronsted-Lowry acid, and the $\text{OH}^-$ formed turns the litmus blue.

**Combine to choose the row**

Ammonium ion behaves as acid, water behaves as acid.

That acid-acid combination matches the correct row.

options.A: Incorrect. The first part is right, $\text{NH}_4^+$ is an acid, but water is not a base here. Water donates $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{NH}_3$ to form $\text{OH}^-$, so water is the acid, not the base.
options.B: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ donates a proton to $\text{OH}^-$ to give $\text{NH}_3$, so it is a Bronsted-Lowry acid. On the paper, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ donates a proton to $\text{NH}_3$ to give $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$, so water is also a Bronsted-Lowry acid.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{NH}_4^+$ does not accept a proton, it donates one to become $\text{NH}_3$, so it cannot be a base. This choice reverses the role in the test tube reaction.
options.D: Incorrect. Neither species is a base in these steps. $\text{NH}_4^+$ is a proton donor and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is a proton donor to $\text{NH}_3$. This is the common trap of thinking water making $\text{OH}^-$ means it acted as a base.
